items.topic: Acamprosate — maintain abstinence after stopping alcohol; use with counseling
items.stem: A client with alcohol use disorder who has stopped drinking is prescribed acamprosate with counseling. Which teaching point is most accurate?

options.text: Acamprosate is used with counseling to help maintain abstinence after drinking has stopped
Acamprosate alone replaces the need for counseling or psychosocial support
Acamprosate is the first treatment for active alcohol withdrawal seizures
Crushing the delayed-release tablets improves absorption and is preferred

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: acamprosate is used with counseling/social support to help people who have stopped drinking avoid drinking again. Merck: medications (including acamprosate) should be used with counseling; acamprosate is a first-line option that may decrease relapse.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize counseling/psychosocial support with medication, not medication alone.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Acamprosate is for maintenance of abstinence after stopping, not acute withdrawal seizure treatment.
rationales.D: Incorrect. MedlinePlus: swallow tablets whole; do not split, chew, or crush.

items.topic: Postpartum psychosis — psychiatric emergency; hallucinations/delusions require urgent evaluation/hospitalization
items.stem: On postpartum day 3, a client has new auditory hallucinations and delusional beliefs about harming the infant. Which nursing interpretation and action priority is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat as a psychiatric emergency: ensure safety and arrange urgent psychiatric evaluation/hospitalization as indicated
Reassure that this is expected baby blues that always resolves without evaluation within 48 hours
Advise waiting two weeks before any mental-health referral because EPDS screening is only done then
Discharge home with only a follow-up phone call in one month and no safety plan

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: postpartum psychosis is an emergency (homicide/infanticide/suicide risk) and may require inpatient care. Merck: hallucinations/delusions/psychotic behavior → evaluate for postpartum psychosis; treatment typically requires psychiatric hospitalization and antipsychotics.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Baby blues are milder and self-limited; psychosis is rare and dangerous—not 'expected blues.'
rationales.C: Incorrect. Psychotic symptoms require immediate evaluation, not a two-week delay.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Unsafe; urgent evaluation and safety measures are required.

items.topic: Braden Scale — lower total score indicates higher pressure-injury risk
items.stem: When interpreting a Braden Scale total score for pressure-injury risk, which statement is correct?

options.text: A lower total score indicates a higher risk of pressure injury
A lower total score always means the client has no risk
Only the friction/shear subscale is used; the total score is ignored
Higher total scores always mean Stage 4 injury is already present

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: the lower the score, the greater the risk. AHRQ: a lower score indicates higher levels of risk; ≤18 generally indicates at-risk status.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lower scores mean higher risk, not no risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Six subscales are totaled; clinical judgment also matters, but the total score is used.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Braden Scale estimates risk; it does not stage an existing injury.

items.topic: Tracheostomy suctioning — limit pass duration; intermittent suction; sterile open technique
items.stem: When performing open tracheostomy suctioning for thick secretions the client cannot clear, which practice is most appropriate?

options.text: Limit each suction pass (do not exceed about 15 seconds), use intermittent suction, and maintain sterile technique for the catheter
Apply continuous suction for several uninterrupted minutes to clear all secretions at once
Never suction through a tracheostomy tube; only suction the mouth
Suction on a fixed schedule every 5 minutes even when the airway is clear

rationales.A: Correct. Open RN/NCBI: do not suction more than 15 seconds per pass; sterile catheter/gloves for open suction; suction when indicated. Merck: suction can be inserted through a tracheostomy; apply intermittent bursts (2–5 seconds).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Prolonged continuous suctioning increases hypoxemia/complication risk; limit pass duration and use intermittent suction.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Merck and Open RN both describe suctioning through a tracheostomy tube.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Open RN: suction when clinically indicated, not indiscriminately on a rigid timer when clear.

items.topic: AV fistula — no BP/IV/blood draws on access arm; assess thrill/bruit
items.stem: A client has a mature arteriovenous (AV) fistula in the left forearm for hemodialysis. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: Do not use the access arm for blood pressure, IVs, or blood draws; check the thrill daily
Prefer the fistula arm for all blood pressures because the pulse is stronger
Sleep only on the access arm to protect the fistula
Ignore loss of the thrill because it is a normal finding overnight

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: do not let anyone take BP, start an IV, or draw blood from the access arm; check thrill daily. OpenStax Skills: no BP cuffs/tourniquets on that arm; no BP/IVFs/blood draws on the affected side; assess thrill/bruit and report if absent.
rationales.B: Incorrect. BP on the access arm is contraindicated.
rationales.C: Incorrect. MedlinePlus: do not sleep on the access arm.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Loss/slowing of thrill requires prompt contact with the provider.

items.topic: NGN cloze — AV fistula: no BP/IV on access arm; check thrill
items.stem: Complete the hemodialysis access teaching for a client with an AV fistula.

ngn.template: Do not use the access arm for {B1}. Check the {B2} daily and contact the provider if it is {B3}.

B1.text: blood pressure, IVs, or blood draws

B2.text: capillary refill only on the opposite foot

B3.text: stronger after sleeping on that arm

rationales.B1a: Correct. No BP/IV/blood draws on the access arm (MedlinePlus/OpenStax).
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is important but is not the access-arm restriction taught here.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Oral medications are unrelated to protecting the fistula arm.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Access assessment focuses on thrill/bruit of the fistula.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Not an AV fistula assessment.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Call if thrill slows or is absent.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Present/unchanged thrill is reassuring, not a call trigger.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Clients should not sleep on the access arm; stronger thrill is not the teaching point for calling.

items.topic: SIADH — fluid/water restriction as core treatment; monitor sodium/I&O
items.stem: A euvolemic client with SIADH has hyponatremia. Which collaborative/nursing priority is most appropriate for mild symptoms?

options.text: Implement prescribed fluid/water restriction and monitor intake/output and serum sodium
Encourage free water intake of several litres daily to flush ADH
Stop all sodium monitoring because SIADH does not affect sodium
Immediately give hypotonic IV fluids to lower sodium further

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: treatment includes fluid/water restriction. OpenStax: oral fluid restriction for mild hyponatremia; nurse monitors I&O, weights, labs/sodium.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Excess free water worsens hyponatremia in SIADH.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hyponatremia is the key result of SIADH and must be monitored.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Hypotonic fluids can worsen hyponatremia; severe symptoms may need careful hypertonic saline, not hypotonic fluids.

items.topic: Opioid overdose — give naloxone and call emergency services; stay with the person
items.stem: A bystander finds an adult with suspected opioid overdose and slowed/stopped breathing. Naloxone is available. Which action sequence is best?

options.text: Call emergency services (911), administer naloxone, and stay with the person until help arrives
Wait 30 minutes to see if breathing improves before giving naloxone or calling for help
Give naloxone and immediately leave so the person can sleep alone
Avoid naloxone because it is harmful if the overdose is not opioid-related

rationales.A: Correct. Health Canada: call 911 and administer naloxone if available. CDC: give naloxone and stay until emergency help arrives (or at least four hours); call 911.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delay risks death; naloxone and emergency activation are urgent.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC: stay with the person; effects can wear off and breathing may stop again (Health Canada).
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC: naloxone will not harm someone overdosing on non-opioids; use if overdose is suspected.
